teach.title: The third family of nouns
teach.say: Most Latin nouns that do not end in -a or -us or -um belong to a third family: **a 3rd-declension noun (the -is / -ēs pattern: pāstor, pāstōris)**, *dēclīnātiō tertia*. Their first form can end in almost anything — *pāstor*, *ovis*, *canis*, *clāmor*, *mōns* — so you cannot tell one by its look alone. Masculine and feminine nouns of this family share every ending, so the gender has to be learned with the word.

teach.title: The genitive shows the stem
teach.say: Because the first form is unreliable, these nouns are learned in pairs: *pāstor, pāstōris*; *arbor, arboris*; *ovis, ovis*. The second form is the genitive (the 'of' form), it always ends **-is**, and what is left when you take that -is off is the stem every other ending is built on: *pāstōr-*, *arbor-*. Some stems change a good deal — *mōns, montis*; *dēns, dentis*. For more than one owner the genitive ends **-um** after most stems and **-ium** after nouns like *ovis* and *collis*: *pāstōrum*, *ovium*.

teach.title: As the object: stem + -em
teach.say: When one of these nouns is what the verb acts on, it goes into the accusative (the object form): add **-em** to the stem — *pānem*, *ovem*, *montem*, *pāstōrem*. The -em is the surest sign of the family in these chapters: nothing you have met so far ends that way except a third-declension object. And no neuter noun ever ends in -em, so a word in -em is masculine or feminine.

teach.title: Receiving with -ī, and -e for the rest
teach.say: Two more singular endings go on the same stem. The dative (the receiver form) is **-ī**: *canī pānem dat*, he gives his dog bread. The ablative (the 'by/with/from' form) is **-e**: *sub arbore*, *in valle*. Keep them apart by their length as much as by their shape: -ī is long, -e is short.

teach.title: Two plural endings, four jobs
teach.say: Once the stem is known, the plural has only two endings left, and each of them does two jobs. **-ēs** is both the nominative (the subject form) and the accusative (the object form): *ovēs herbam edunt*, *dentēs magnōs habet*. **-ibus** is both the dative (the receiver form) and the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form): *pāstor canibus et ovibus aquam dat*. Two endings to learn, and the sentence tells you which job each is doing.

teach.title: The trap: -is and -īs
teach.say: *Ovis* can be the nominative (the subject form: one sheep) or the genitive (the owner form) of the very same word, and it looks like nothing in the other declensions — but *servīs* with a long ī is a second-declension plural, not this family at all. In *dominus servīs aquam dat, pāstor ovibus* the two plurals do the same job with different endings, because the nouns come from different families. Check the dictionary pair before you decide.

core.text: Most Latin nouns that do not end in -a, -us or -um belong to the third declension: **a 3rd-declension noun (the -is / -es pattern: pastor, pastoris)**, *dēclīnātiō tertia*. Its first form can end in almost anything — *pāstor*, *ovis*, *rēx*, *homō* — so the form to remember is the genitive (the 'of' form) in -is, which shows the stem: *pāstor, pāstōr-is*; *rēx, rēg-is*. Every other ending goes onto that stem: *pāstōrem*, *pāstōrī*, *pāstōre*; plural *pāstōrēs*, *pāstōrum*, *pāstōribus*.
A few English nouns change their stem in the plural (*mouse / mice*, *foot / feet*). Latin third-declension nouns change it in every form but the first, so they are learned in pairs.
Learn nominative, genitive and gender together (*ovis, ovis f*). Endings: -em, -is, -ī, -e; plural -ēs, -um / -ium, -ibus. Masculine and feminine share them all.

invented.en: The dog keeps the sheep safe from the wolf.
The king gives the soldiers money.

core.text: Neuter third-declension nouns (*flūmen*, *mare*, *animal*) use the same endings but, like every neuter, keep nominative = accusative and take -a (or -ia) in the plural: *flūmina*, *maria*. A word in -ēs or -em used as the object is masculine or feminine; a neuter object never ends in -em.

more.text: From the learner's notes: the course calls these is-nouns; some (*carō*, *rēx*) have a stem change that must be memorised, and the endings are always added to the changed stem (*carnem*, *rēgem*); the genitive plural is -(i)um, the ablative singular -e (occasionally -ī). The is-noun pattern is only masculine or feminine; neuters follow their own pattern. Genders must be committed to memory: *pānis* m, *carō* f.

Ørberg cap. IX declines the three declensions side by side: *īnsula*, *servus*, *pāstor* / *ovis*. A nominative in -s often hides a consonant: *rēx* = *rēg-s*, *pēs, pedis*, *vōx, vōcis*; *homō, hominis*. Genitive plural -ium belongs to nouns like *ovis, ovium* and *collis, collium*; -um to *pāstor, pāstōrum* and *homō, hominum*. Rules of thumb: -or and -ō are masculine (*pāstor*, *timor*, *homō*; but *carō* f), -is and -ēs mostly feminine (but *pānis*, *canis*, *collis* m; and *mōns, montis* m). Beware -is: *ovis* is nominative or genitive singular, while *servīs* is dative or ablative plural of the 2nd declension. A&G §64–72.
